reference.source: Oxford Textbook of Endocrinology and Diabetes
clinicalPearls: Osteomalacia is impaired mineralisation of newly formed osteoid in the mature skeleton; the childhood equivalent, affecting the growth plate, is rickets.
The commonest cause worldwide is vitamin D deficiency (nutritional, malabsorption, limited sunlight); hypophosphataemia and mineralisation inhibitors are important non-calcipenic causes.
Classic biochemistry is low or low-normal calcium, low phosphate, raised alkaline phosphatase, raised PTH and low 25-hydroxyvitamin D.
Diffuse bone pain with a proximal myopathy (waddling gait, difficulty rising from a chair) is characteristic, often with bony tenderness on sternal or tibial pressure.
Looser zones (pseudofractures) on the compression side of long bones, pubic rami, scapula and ribs are a near-pathognomonic radiological feature.
Distinguish calcipenic forms (vitamin D or calcium deficiency, high PTH) from phosphopenic forms (renal phosphate wasting, FGF23-mediated) as treatment differs fundamentally.
Transiliac bone biopsy after tetracycline double-labelling showing increased osteoid thickness and prolonged mineralisation lag time is the gold standard but rarely required.
Hypocalcaemia and hypophosphataemia may worsen transiently when repletion begins ('hungry bone'), so monitor biochemistry during treatment.
reference.pathophysiology: Mature bone is continually remodelled, with osteoblasts laying down unmineralised osteoid that is subsequently mineralised by deposition of calcium and phosphate as hydroxyapatite. In osteomalacia this mineralisation step fails or lags, so accumulating unmineralised osteoid weakens the skeleton. The dominant mechanism is inadequate availability of calcium and phosphate at the mineralising front, most often from vitamin D deficiency (reduced intestinal calcium and phosphate absorption, secondary hyperparathyroidism and renal phosphate loss). Other routes include chronic hypophosphataemia from renal phosphate wasting (FGF23 excess, Fanconi syndrome), renal failure with impaired 1-alpha-hydroxylation, hypophosphatasia (low tissue-non-specific alkaline phosphatase), and inhibitors of mineralisation such as aluminium, fluoride and some bisphosphonates.
additionalDifferentials: metastatic bone disease or multiple myeloma
additionalInvestigations: serum calcium, phosphate and alkaline phosphatase
renal profile with urine phosphate and tubular reabsorption of phosphate (TmP/GFR)
coeliac serology and markers of malabsorption
intact FGF23 where unexplained phosphate wasting is suspected
transiliac bone biopsy with tetracycline labelling in diagnostic uncertainty
redFlags: symptomatic hypocalcaemia (tetany, seizures, prolonged QT interval)
insufficiency fractures, particularly of the femoral neck
severe proximal weakness causing recurrent falls
unexplained renal phosphate wasting raising suspicion of tumour-induced osteomalacia
underlying malabsorption such as coeliac disease or previous bariatric surgery
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is excellent when the underlying deficiency is corrected, with bone pain and proximal myopathy usually resolving over weeks to months. Established skeletal deformity or fractures may leave residual disability.
pitfalls: attributing symptoms to osteoporosis or fibromyalgia and missing osteomalacia
assuming normal serum calcium excludes the diagnosis
failing to seek an underlying malabsorptive cause
not distinguishing calcipenic from phosphopenic mechanisms before treatment
giving vitamin D alone when renal phosphate wasting is the primary problem
references: Oxford Textbook of Endocrinology and Diabetes
management: Correction of the underlying deficiency — in calcipenic disease, vitamin D repletion with colecalciferol or ergocalciferol plus calcium supplementation

For phosphopenic forms, phosphate supplementation with an active vitamin D metabolite such as calcitriol or alfacalcidol, and an anti-FGF23 antibody such as burosumab where FGF23-mediated wasting is confirmed
Treatment of the specific cause, including a gluten-free diet in coeliac disease, active vitamin D analogues in renal impairment, and resection of a causative tumour in tumour-induced osteomalacia
Symptomatic support with analgesia for bone pain and rehabilitation for proximal myopathy
Biochemical monitoring of calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase and parathyroid hormone, adjusting therapy to normalise mineralisation and avoid hypercalcaemia
Orthopaedic management of pseudofractures, completed fractures and skeletal deformity
Referral to metabolic bone specialists for phosphopenic, hereditary or refractory disease
